utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technicians, the interpreters; good morning, legal assistants, court reporters; good morning, representatives of the Registry; good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Cayley, Mr. McCloskey; good morning, Mr. Petrusic; good morning, Mr. Visnjic; and good morning to you, General Krstic. Good morning, Mr. Butler. We are going to continue with your testimony, and let me remind you that you are still under an oath. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; good morning, my learned colleagues from the Prosecution; good morning to all of you present here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I would like to move on to your second chapter, chapter 2, of your report from the month of May. I hope that we will be able to proceed at a somewhat faster pace than yesterday. Mr. Butler, from a military point of view and from the point of view of the VRS, could we say that in the month of July 1995, there were any significant operations for the army of Republika Srpska and the Drina Corps in relation to the operation Krivaja-95? This is, is there any more significant military operations than the military operation Krivaja-95?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically for the month of July 1995, and dealing with the zone of the Drina Corps, the significant military operations would have been Krivaja-95, would have been the follow-on military operation Stupcanica or Stupcanica-95, which was Zepa. It would have been the issue pertaining to the column moving from Srebrenica through the lines towards Tuzla, and it would have been the maintenance of the line of confrontation which the corps maintained throughout the zone of the brigade against the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the material that was available to you, did you come across any fact, any circumstance, or piece of evidence that the Commander of the Drina Corps, up to the day of the appointment of Radislav Krstic to the office of the Commander, that is, that the previous Commander had been in any way prevented to command the corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, sir, what you're asking is did I come across any piece of information that indicates that General Zivanovic was prevented from commanding the corps up to a point in time when General Krstic took over. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was exactly my question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one piece of information that I have that would fit into that, and that is an interview taken with General Zivanovic by a Newsweek press reporter, and in this interview, which again I've been unable to substantiate through my own documents, General Zivanovic notes that he relinquished command of the Drina Corps officially at the headquarters in Vlasenica on 11 July 1995, in the early evening. After that, he goes to the military medical centre in Belgrade. Now, clearly putting that in the context of the fact basis which has been introduced to date, we have General Zivanovic signing orders as the Corps Commander on both the 12th and 13th of July, and we have General Zivanovic active in the zone of the corps in communications on 14 July, and we have the document from president Karadzic indicating that he is, in fact, officially on paper the Commander through 15 July, where he then becomes the -- on disposal to the Main Staff. So, yes, I have that one piece of information. It's unsupported by the rest of the fact base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That piece of information, has it been substantiated in any way in terms of evidence or exhibits that you have analysed and that you have mentioned in your testimony yesterday and today? Do you have any such piece of evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. And as I've indicated, the evidence that has been introduced today refutes that version of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can we say that the composition of the Corps Command is made of the Commander, the staff, and the assistants, the assistants being the assistants of the Commander for the Security, then morale and religious issues, and Assistant Commander for Logistics?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would add the Chief of Staff into that mix, but, yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That would have been the second part of my question. So can we agree with this assertion or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the staff, is it composed of the Chief of Staff and the assistants, Assistant Commanders for Operations, Intelligence Affairs, and also Commanders of special departments or branches of the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, is he in charge of controlling and commanding the staff and coordinating the work of the command in general, of the headquarters in general?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we finally conclude -- or, rather, reach a conclusion as to the duties and authorities of the Chief of Staff, and can we therefore say that the competence is the authority pursuant to the regulations on the authority of the Corps Command in peacetime from 1990 is such authority and such competence that are vested with the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, are you -- you're asking if the 1990 corps regulations are an accurate reflection of the roles and responsibilities of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Those are baseline foundational documents which demonstrate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So that would be the exact roles and responsibilities of the Chief of Staff, nothing more, nothing less than what has been provided for in the regulations that we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that's incorrect. As I've indicated yesterday and on previous testimony, these regulations are baseline foundational documents with which then the corps themselves will articulate instructions on how to accomplish and do the specific tasks. As an example, I use the JNA 4th Corps document which shows how a JNA corps, and later to become a VRS corps, takes those two bulk regulations, those baseline regulations, and in fact makes specific guidance and instructions pertaining to how their corps command and staff will operate. So it will be an unfair statement to say that the regulations as stated are exact, and that in every case, a Chief of Staff or any staff officer would be strictly bound by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is there any legal document which provides that the Chief of Staff would be bound by them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no specific legal document relative to the RS law and defence or the RS law and the army that specifically pertains to what a Chief of Staff is bound or not bound to. However, in reviewing those same laws, it's specific that the soldiers and the officers of the army will follow the regulations and the instructions and the orders of those individuals appointed over them and carry out the instructions as such. So it's a general roll-up, it's not a specific designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to your opinion, was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, that is, did the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps have any large -- any more authority than the authority that is provided for in the said regulations, Regulations On the Authority of the Ground Forces Corps Commander In Peacetime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that he had additional authority, and what I use to back that belief up is the series of exhibits and other things that have come out of the fact base to do that. My belief is that the actual standard that was being applied or that was being exercised is a standard that is reflected in the JNA 4th Corps document pertaining to the roles and responsibilities of the Chief of Staff. And as I had previously noted, the regulations and provisions certainly made account for the fact that in a wartime environment, lessons would be learned, and that those lessons would be applied accordingly; and the JNA document 1991 is published, the 4th Corps document, reflects many of the lessons learned as a result of JNA military operations in Croatia in early 1991. Now, the documents that I have, and there are specific exhibits that demonstrate that, indicate that the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, at that time General Krstic specifically, was giving orders and directions to subordinate brigades that would have, in theory, been over and above the designated competence of such if one goes back and looks at that 1990 document, both the provisional regulations and the peacetime regulations. So, again, the 1990 provisional regulations and peacetime regulations being the foundational documents, and the units as they evolved through a wartime environment, making adjustments to those regulations to suit the combat needs of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the regulations of the 4th Corps is a body of regulations that were issued by the 4th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And let me please finish my question, Mr. Butler. But is it also true that the two corps -- that the Drina Corps has no physical relation, is something completely different than the 4th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've noted that. And again, it is not my intention to infer that the Drina Corps in any way, shape, or form was bound to follow the instructions of another corps. The point that I'm making is the fact that in those specific regulations, the Chief of Staff roles and responsibilities, I see those reflected through the fact basis and my analysis of those being the actual roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, would it be true to say that the doctrine of the former JNA, including the 4th Corps, at the times of the events that took place in Croatia in 1991, that the doctrine was different from the doctrine of the VRS in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would observe that, as I've noted before, while there were changes made to reflect wartime experience, the base doctrine and the base operating methodologies were the foundation of how the VRS conducted combat in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your report in paragraph 2.10 on page 13, you speak about the Chief Commander. I must say that I am -- when you say Chief Commander or the Main Commander, the Defence is somewhat confused, and we think that you probably want to say that there are some additional, some other, Commanders. Can we conclude from your statement here that there would be some kind of dual or concurrent command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that in this case, we're both victims of a bad translation between English and B/C/S. What I'm noting in this case, and the phrase that I use in English, is the overall commander, and in the cases where you have groupings of multiple forces, one individual is appointed to be in command of the groupings of forces. That is the overall or, in my mind, the Superior Commander of those groupings of forces. So in this case, I think we're the victims of a bad translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I should like the situation to be that way. So that can refer to the Commander-in-Chief of the area in question and during the relevant times, that is, the times you are discussing in your report. Mr. Butler, am I correct in understanding you, that you are referring to the Commander-in-Chief in a specific place at a specific time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I would not use the phrase "Commander-in-Chief." In my vocabulary, the phrase "Commander-in-Chief" would roughly equate to either the president of the republic or the Commander of the Main Staff, and I don't want to make that designation. What I am saying is that when I use the phrase "the overall commander" in a series of groupings where various military units are grouped together and an individual commander is designated, and maybe the best way to explain this is to refer back to the Main Staff order of 17 July 1995, whereas part of that order a group of units were identified, a specific zone was articulated, and then a specific individual, a Colonel Keserovic, I believe, was identified as the Commander of those groupings of forces, and that is the context in which I'm trying to place the phrase "overall commander" in, those types of groupings, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When the four provisional types of command were established in the month of July, or four temporary command relationships, as you refer to them in 2.11, does that mean that the unity of command was impaired in any way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe impaired, but these temporary command groupings, in some cases, were resubordinated to a formation outside the Drina Corps or were resubordinated in operating under the Drina Corps control. So while command responsibility for some of these groups shifted outside of the corps, I wouldn't use the phrase "impaired" in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the role of the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and bearing in mind the regulations, would any different type of role in any way endanger the principle of the unity of command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the Chief of Staff and putting it into the context of, for example, July 1995, we have the example of during the operation Krivaja-95, the Chief of Staff was in charge of or commanded the tactical portion of the operation against Srebrenica until that point in time when General Zivanovic and General Mladic showed up. And even after that period he was actually the person responsible for the specific directives to the brigades. He was in command of those formational units and directing their activities during the period he was still the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander. General Mladic was the Commander of the Main Staff. So I don't see how a circumstance in that regard would or could be potentially interpreted as something improper within the framework of unity of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Commander of the Main Staff is equivalent to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm sorry. Commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that case, that is, during the period from the 6th until the 11th of July, did the Chief of Staff obey orders of his superior, that is, the Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's a factual statement, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does that follow from the stand that only the Commander has the competence to command unless he transfers that authority to his subordinate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Commander, as articulated under the body of regulations, instructions, and other orders, is the sole authority to command the corps at that level. And while the regulations and the instructions and other orders allow for him to delegate authority down to other officers to include the Chief of Staff, to include Assistant Commanders, to include other staff officers, for that matter, it specifies that he, the Commander, retains the responsibility for the actions of those subordinates in those command positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the unit, the 65th Protective Motorised Regiment [sic] based in Nova Kasaba or, rather, with the command post in Nova Kasaba, was a unit of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit in question was the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. It was in Nova Kasaba. It was directly subordinate to the Commander and command of the 65th Protection Regiment, and that regiment was directly subordinate to the Main Staff of the VRS, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is there any evidence to prove that after the 15th of July, during the search of the terrain south of the Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba road that crimes were committed in that area during the sweep-up operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to that would be that while I'm not going to qualify whether it is or is not evidence, I have information from the Bratunac daily combat reports which indicates that numbers of other prisoners were taken by the Bratunac Brigade units in that area through July, through August, through September, and we've demonstrated and put in those documents as exhibits. We don't have qualified numbers of how many people were taken as part of those sweep operations, and we don't have hard facts because there were none taken by the brigade as to names or locations as to what the ultimate disposition of these people who were captured in the sweep operations or what happened to them. So again, I can't qualify it as evidence, but I certainly have a fact base which shows that prisoners were being taken in those areas after the date in question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel or Lieutenant-Colonel Ignjac Milanovic -- please correct me if I'm wrong -- addressed a proposal to the Corps Commander -- I'm referring to Exhibit 537 -- in which he makes certain suggestions as to how a military tactical situation on the ground should be addressed. Do we have any evidence to show that the Corps Commander acted in accordance with those suggestions or, to put it differently, that he accepted that proposal and naturally translated it into an order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could wait for a few seconds, sir. I believe they're getting me the exhibit now. Okay, sir, in reference to your question, and again, you specifically designated, you know, this in response to the Corps Commander on 15 July, working under the premise that General-Major Krstic is the Corps Commander on that date, what we see here is first in accordance to your orders, a very specific designation. We also note that it's sent to the corps IKM to the attention of the Commander. Taking this, and I won't revisit the series of instructions in it, what I've concluded is that if you review the Bratunac Brigade daily combat report for 16 July 1995, and I do not know the exhibit number of that offhand, that that combat report reflects the series of applications which I infer to a decision being made, and further, how the Brigade Commander is carrying out those activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 539 for the -- if it's considered needed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I noted earlier, those are indicated in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is this proposal in line with military regulations regarding conduct in the area of combat operations, and generally under the circumstances in which the Bratunac Brigade found itself after the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this reflects not the Bratunac Brigade, but this reflects the series of circumstances which the Drina Corps found itself after 11, 12 July, and in this specific case, the circumstances of 15, 16 July 1995. So I wouldn't limit it to the Bratunac Brigade at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When I said the Bratunac Brigade, I had meant that these activities were taking place in the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The activities occurring in that scope of the area, while a large portion were in the zone of the brigade, it was not exclusively within the zone of brigade, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can it be said that the operation Krivaja-95 was completed on the 11th of July at about 1800 hours at the time when the units and the Command Officers of the Drina Corps entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have the information that would specifically allow me to answer an exact day and time the operation ended. The only broad inferences that I can make would be that in one instance, presumably the operation would end prior to the beginning of the following operations Stupcanica-95, although that does not necessarily have to be the case; you can run multiple operations simultaneously. And I would further refer you back to the comment by Colonel Pandurevic in one of his interim combat reports -- and memory fails me. It's either the 15th or the 16th I believe -- where he specifically notes that he doesn't consider the operation Krivaja-95 completed until after all of the issues are dealt with in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your military, practical, and theoretical expertise, and the positions of your military doctrine, the system you belong to, what is meant when it is said that an operation has been completed, and when does it actually come to an end?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very broad question. There is no formula for that. In many cases, in a finite sense, in terms of time, an operation ends at a given date and time that's specified in the order. If the goal of the operation is the destruction of a force or the seizure of an objective, it ends upon the completion of those missions. I guess the broadest way to put it is, the operation ends when the Commander declares that the mission is completed. There's no fixing of date, time, or circumstances, other than a designation by the Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could you tell us whether there is any act, any document, Command document, whereby the special MUP Brigade or Police Brigade was placed under the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that instance, the document that I would refer back to is the Krivaja-95 operations order which indicates as part of the reserve forces of the Drina Corps, that two or three companies of MUP forces will be part of that. Based on where we've discussed on the issue of reserve, I infer that to be that those three companies are operating under the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the order that you are referring to, those three companies are in the reserve?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are dedicated -- they are designated as the corps reserve, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do we have any evidence to show that those three companies were actively deployed in combat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that I do not have the Drina Corps orders or combat logbook which reflects their orders and operations for that, there's no way that I can say at what point in time they were or were not deployed. The best that I can note pertaining to that is witness testimony and the video exhibits which show the MUP Police in the Srebrenica area and along the Bratunac-Potocari Road 11 -- I'm sorry, 12, 13 July 1995, and references to their continued presence and other Drina Corps or Bratunac Brigade specific documents through the 15th and 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the same principle of inference can be used for the cessation of activities by MUP units in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, that is, the termination of their deployment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I don't understand what you're asking me. Could you ask me the question or rephrase it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You have told us that you have no documents of the Drina Corps to show when those units were deployed in the operation that was ongoing in the area. My question is, do you know when the need to deploy those units ceased, when there was no longer any need for them to be deployed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, because I don't have the documents, I would be unable to give any form of a judgement as to when the exact date would be, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we now come to chapter 3 of your expert opinion. In your opinion, and on the basis of your analytical work about which you testified in the examination-in-chief, did the UNPROFOR members fully execute their obligations as provided for by the resolution of the Security Council and the agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica -- or rather, of the safe area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me a question way over my pay grade, sir. I don't believe that I can make a judgement as to whether or not a particular UN force fulfilled its mandate as required by the UN. That's over my scope of expertise, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'm sorry, I really didn't have that in mind in preparing for this cross-examination, but I came across one of your conclusions in studying your report, and that is what prompted this question. Let us leave the United Nations aside. But could you tell us, did the Muslims respect the obligations emanating from the UN resolution and, of course, from the agreement, the signed agreement on demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the information basis which we forwarded to date reflects the fact that Muslim armed military units continued to operate out of the safe area, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I am now referring to the presence of General Zivanovic, referred to in paragraph 3.6, in the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, and my question has to do with the 3rd and 4th of July. In the combat and tactical rules on the deployment of units in the military that you come from, are such activities provided for as customary, as a regular component part of the operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what you're referring to and what I'm referencing here is what in the JNA, as adopted by VRS doctrine, is called the Commander's reconnaissance, in which the Commander, in many cases, physically takes his subordinate Commanders to a position where they can overlook the battlefield, and they will discuss, as part of the planning process, what steps are to be taken, what steps are not to be taken. I can say that we have a similar Commander's reconnaissance as part of the US army doctrine as well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So this is something that is quite legitimate, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And it applies to both the Commander and the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can the Chief of Staff, as part of the organisation of the corps, have the right to issue preparatory orders and information so that the units can prepare in the best possible manner for the execution of assignments and carry out the orders of the Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preparatory orders are, and again as I've testified, are a normal and expected part of a military operation in order to allow subordinate units to -- they are the time to gather the necessary resources prior to the actual conduct of an operation or to even -- even prior to the actual receiving of the operations plan. I believe the regulations note -- I believe they note that the Commander is responsible for publishing the preparations order. However, again it wouldn't be uncommon for the Chief of Staff to publish a preparations order if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After this preparations order comes the order of the Commander for active combat, this order being within the competence of the Commander, in this case, the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order again actually assembled and all the portions of it, and if you go back and understand through the JNA documents and the VRS documents how the actual command and staff planning process works, it is a very formalised process, particularly with respect to large orders, where the staff organs and functions coordinate their activities, and this process occurs under the direction of Chief of Staff. The end result of this process is the presentation to the Commander of various military options to achieve the goal that the Commander has designated. After the Commander chooses the designated option that he wants to exercise, the staff turns around and takes that option and publishes it as an order to be executed by the brigades and the remainder of the corps units. So I didn't want to oversimplify the process, but essentially what you're saying is essentially correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in the course of your analytical work, did you come across any more precise or detailed information or data about the strength of the 28th Division, its structure, its composition, its weaponry, generally the elements that characterise a military unit such as the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, if you look at the Krivaja-95 OP order, the beginning paragraphs of that OP order specifically outline the Drina Corps's understanding of the enemy dispositions in the enclave. Further to that, as you asked what other data I possessed, we had the limited records of the 28th Division that were captured by the Drina Corps, the Zvornik Brigade specifically, at Srebrenica and were in the custody of the VRS for several years before we, in effect, reseized them back, and we have some documents that come from the Milici Brigade which further outline their view of the Muslim strength and military compositions within the enclave. So I believe that the documents indicate that the VRS had a good understanding of the enemy that they faced inside the enclave, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 9th of July, the Muslim military and civilian leadership decided to abandon the enclave. This is paragraph 3.12.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In paragraph 3.11.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're right. I'm sorry. 3.11.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 3.11, what I say is that by the evening of 9 July, the situation was rapidly becoming critical for the Muslim civilians and military leadership in Srebrenica. I believe, as I've previously discussed, my understanding is the decision by the Muslim military and civilian leadership to abandon the enclave occurred on the evening of 10 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In view of that decision, the decision which was substantiated in Exhibit 404/2, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could I have your assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So in view of this decision dated 9 July, reached in the evening hours of that date, was it to be expected -- was anything else -- could anything else be expected from the Serbian army except from their entering an empty town?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you asking me what my view of the expectations of the VRS would be pertaining to when they -- what the circumstances would be when they entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: If we have in mind the decision that had been reached, and also if we bear in mind the fact that the Muslim population was abandoning the city and withdrawing in the direction of Potocari, was any other decision of the Drina Corps -- would any other decision of the Drina Corps be reasonable except from the decision to enter an abandoned, empty town?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I understand your question. The first thing that I would point out is that, again, this being a Bosnian Muslim document from a Serb municipality, I would in no way enter that the VRS gained possession of this document prior to or anywhere as part of the 9 July decision-making process. So this is an unknown fact to the army of the Republika Srpska. Secondly, as indicated by the previous testimony, the forward command post of the Drina Corps had excellent line of sight. The army was in the hills and the town is in the valley. They had good visual observation of the town, and, as such, they should have had a good indication of what the state of the town was, and the reports being received from their units pertaining to whether or not the town was going to be defended or what the status of the civilian population or -- excuse me -- what the status and location of the UN forces would be. So given all of that, and particularly with respect to exhibit, this is an after the fact piece of information that I would not assume that the VRS knew about on 9 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But in any case, in view of the position of the RKM and the intelligence data and everything else that was followed by the army of Republika Srpska in terms of events that were taking place in Srebrenica, it is obvious that at one point in time they did have knowledge and information that the town was abandoned, that it was empty, that is, that the Muslim population was withdrawing from the town.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best that I can say is that certainly by the evening of 9 July 1995, and again based on the directive from the Supreme Commander, president Karadzic, and again based on the success to date of the operation by the army of Republika Srpska, the military was given permission to continue to advance in the town. What one reads back from that is speculation, but certainly the circumstances existed, to the knowledge of the president, that now the goal of actually taking the town was open to them and they chose that option.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Units of the 10th Sabotage Detachment were also spotted in Srebrenica. I think we can agree on that assertion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. They were identified there over the foothills where they arrived on 10 July, and they were in the town on 11 July, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the 10th Detachment or, rather, the number of soldiers of the 10th Detachment, was that number of soldiers such a significant military asset that was -- that would have been indispensable to the units that were taking part in the attack on the takeover of Srebrenica for the purpose of those specific military operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, sir, now you're asking me to comment on the military judgement of certainly General Krstic and General Mladic, individuals who have many more years of leading troops than I do. What I would say, though, is that given the fact that the mission objective had now changed to essentially trying to physically occupy an urban area, given the fact that within a military context of the attack, urban area combat certainly in the US army doctrine is considered to be one of the most difficult, dangerous, and high casualty potential operations, and given the fact that the members of the 10th Diversionary Unit were in fact extremely highly trained soldiers, the addition of even the limited number of those soldiers to the actual units that were going to assault the town would not have been an unreasonable addition for any military commander to want to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, would this perhaps be a convenient for you to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, speaking of the character and composition of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, which was a reconnaissance and sabotage unit in its nature intended for combat activities inside the enemy territory, and in view of that fact, can we conclude that the unit, as such, could not be made part of the combat operations in Srebrenica on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would refer back to the statements and testimony of Drazan Erdemovic which, in fact, indicates that the 10th Diversionary Unit was operating as part of the Drina Wolves, the Zvornik Infantry Brigade elements, that conducted combat on 11 July. They became part of that unit, or were at least tactically attached to that unit in the evening of 10th July. I wouldn't conclude that at all, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your research, did you come across a piece of evidence which would support the fact that the Main Staff of that unit was resubordinated to one of the units of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As translated, your question reads to me "the Main Staff of that unit," and I don't understand, what unit is that that we're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: There has obviously been a misunderstanding. Do we have any evidence that the Main Staff of the VRS had resubordinated the 10th Sabotage Detachment to a unit of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a specific document relative to the operations orders or anything of that nature which indicates that the 10th Diversionary was resubordinated to the Drina Corps for that aspect of the operation. Again, I draw my conclusion based on the testimony of Drazan Erdemovic and the fact that how they tactically operated as part of that unit, the military judgement would be that they are, in fact, attached to the unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the events in and around Srebrenica were taking place throughout the war and since 1992 up until 1995, and I will take the liberty and conclude that Srebrenica was, strategically speaking, a problem -- a thorn in the thigh of the army of the Republika Srpska. Bearing in mind the fact that even before the relevant times, certain events had happened involving Srebrenica, can we say that as early as the 10th of July when it was obvious that the VRS would enter Srebrenica, that everybody wanted to end up as a winner, as a victor in that combat, including, of course, the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "everyone," I will assume that you're talking about the army of the Republika Srpska side of everyone. The conclusion that you've noted is that everyone wanted to be there or to be seen to be there at the eve of a significant victory, and I would say that certainly the physical appearance of Mladic showing up at that time supports that conclusion, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question referred to the units, Mr. Butler, including the 10th Sabotage Detachment and the police as well.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, that while individuals and commanders may want to show up and be part of the publicity programme, I would not credit that to military units. The 10th Diversionary in and of itself does not show up at a designated point on the battle for a photo opportunity. Taking that aside in a military complex -- or context, even, is the fact that, remembering that there are still significant combat activities occurring, the VRS does not have a clear indication of where the Muslim 28th Division is and what its future intentions are; and as, you know, their own forces are operating in the battlefield, and we're talking about an environment with a lot of life ordnance going both ways, military units just don't show up unannounced and in undesignated zones. That's a real easy way to get a lot of your own people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From the establishment of the IKM at Pribicevac for the purposes of the operation Krivaja-1995, did you come across a piece of evidence as to which Commanding Officers of the Drina Corps were present at that location from the 4th of July onwards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have several pieces of information pertaining to that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As regards the information of the 4th of July, do you know the composition of the Command staff at the Pribicevac forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before answering your question, sir, and keeping in mind the agreement that the Prosecution and you have made pertaining to some parts of information, I would request that we go into closed session to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would support Mr. Butler on that. I'm not precisely sure, of course, what his answer is, but I think it would be on the safe side if we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Registrar tells me that we are already in public session. You may continue, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we are now discussing chapter 4 of your report. The date is the 11th of July. In your opinion, the directive of the president, Mr. Karadzic, number 01-1340, on the appointment of Deronjic as the civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica, that directive, as regards the duties, the responsibilities, and the authority pursuant to that decision, to that directive, would you doctor that directive to be ambiguous or perhaps contradictory in certain of its portions? I'm referring to footnote number 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Exhibit number 404/2, footnote number 90.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, I would say that the information is relatively specific. However, I would note that the investigation has gained information that indicates that certainly the individual in question was less than clear about his role, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The information that you mention is not available to us, that is, they cannot be found within the materials submitted as evidence, as supporting material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that sounds like a statement to the Prosecution more than it does to the witness, and we can discuss that, and if we want to discuss this topic, there's many other -- there are other investigative materials, of course, that have not been provided to the Defence, and if we are going to discuss those issues, we prefer that it be done in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, I will withdraw my question. If later on we have to move into private session, I will bring up the issue again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. You may continue with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in that presidential decree was there any mention of the Drina Corps? I'm not referring to specific individuals, so I think you can give me an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no specific reference to the Drina Corps in this document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I should now like to go on to discuss the meeting of the 11th of July, in the evening, about 10.00, attended by representatives of the Muslim authorities and the Commander of the Dutch Battalion, as well as representatives of the military and civilian authorities of Republika Srpska. At that meeting, General Mladic, on behalf of the party he represents, has the main say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a representative of the army of Republika Srpska, General Mladic is doing most of the talking, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The other commanding officers of the Drina Corps are present, who, without any exceptions, are all quiet; they are silent. Is that correct? Or, rather, they do not take part in any of the discussions at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On that day and at that time, General Krstic was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, wasn't he? Wasn't he? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At that meeting and during that time, I believe he was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, Mr. Butler, relative to everything that was said by General Mladic, if the Drina Corps command did not agree with that, would the Corps Commander have to express that disagreement or the Chief of Staff, in the event that they disagreed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That being an individual military-style judgement call, if you were, there are two possible courses of action which I could conceive of. The first one would be that specific disagreements, General Krstic as the Chief of Staff would take them to General Zivanovic as the Corps Commander, request guidance and explain where he understands the problems to lie. If the disagreements were of a minor nature and did not have to do with either substantive policy issues and just perhaps reflected a misunderstanding about the abilities or the resources of the corps to do something, then General Krstic, as the Chief of Staff, could, presumably after the meeting, remind General Mladic that because of other orders and considerations that they would be either unable to carry out some tasks or that in order to carry out some tasks they would have to suspend others. How the individual officer in question chose to deal with those issues would be very much circumstance dependent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I understand you, as discussing the individual reactions and their individual positions, but if you view the corps as an institution, which it is, which has its own Commander, and bearing in mind the rights and duties of that Commander, would that be the obligation of the Commander to express any such disagreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would refer back to depending on the context of the disagreement, and I'm also placing it in the military context of the Chief of Staff. For example, an issue where the Chief of Staff might be very knowledgeable pertaining to the amount of resources needed to move people from point "A" to point "B," he might very well immediately know what the answer is, that they can or cannot support that, and would conceivably take the opportunity to remind the general, in this case General Mladic in question, that, "Sir, you realise what you said that if we're going to do that, we'll need additional resources." But again, those are minor technical issues. In a certain major -- on major related issues, and I won't speculate on to what the qualifying line would be, certainly the Chief of Staff would be -- the most appropriate course of action for him would be to go to the Corps Commander and express his disagreement with the course of action that has been articulated by the Superior Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You're placing this in the context of the Chief of Staff, but can you also place that within the context of the Corps Commander and his role and attitude towards the same issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object at this point as to vagueness, Your Honour. These discussions are so open ended that the answers are not relevant and are -- in many cases the questions aren't, for vagueness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, the objection is unfounded in view of the fact that Mr. Butler is referring to the Chief of Staff context. I'm just asking him to give me the same answer with relation to the Corps Commander in relation to the same problem. I think the question was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, any additional remarks to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, continue, please, with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Butler, do I need to repeat the question? In the context of the Corps Commander, what would be the attitude of the Corps Commander relating to any objections he may have and any disagreement with what the Commander of the Main Staff has said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without commenting on an individual's mental state or attitude, with the respect of the Corps Commander, conceivably he has a similar series of options. The first option would be to approach the superior in his case, the Supreme Commander or Superior Commander in this case, and since we're talking corps, let's put a name "General Mladic" on it just so we don't get confused, and express the fact that either he disagrees with the course of action or that he agrees with the course of action, but just does not have the required resources to carry out an activity. With regards to another avenue, it would not be unusual for a Corps Commander to approach General Mladic's staff, the Main Staff, and indicate that for a variety of reasons, he may or may not be able to comply with certain orders. And again, I don't want to speculate what those reasons can and cannot be, but that is a legitimate avenue of approach to him in order to deal with militarily fundamental issues. I suspect his third avenue of recourse, the other two either failing and depending on how strongly the individual Commander in question felt about an issue, that he has the option of availing himself to his Superior Commander, which in the case of a Corps Commander, General Mladic's boss, that would be the President of the republic. And again, without context and without speculating as to what the individual rationale would be, those would be, in my mind, the three broad categories or avenues that he would have open to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpreter] Could I ask Exhibit 404/2, footnote 20, to be placed onto the ELMO, the report of the Dutch, the Dutch Battalion, paragraph 514.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, bearing in mind the telegram Mr. Akashi sent to the Security Council of the UN regarding the transport and evacuation of refugees, and his proposals that efforts must be made to reach agreement with the army of Republika Srpska to allow the entire population of the enclave, including all men, to depart for Tuzla, and this is dated the 11th of July, what would be your position regarding the legal characterisation of the charge of deportation in the indictment in view of this, in this context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Calling for a legal conclusion which is not appropriate for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding a legal conclusion, I agree with the objection; but regarding the facts, my question is, do these facts in any way influence the position of Mr. Butler regarding the evacuation or resettlement of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Petrusic, I gave you the floor to respond to Mr. McCloskey's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't really have a problem with his second question, as long as he's not asking Mr. Butler to comment on charges in the indictment. I don't think we should get that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You heard the remark of the Prosecution. You can ask the question, but without asking for any legal conclusions from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I accepted the objection made by Mr. McCloskey regarding any legal conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So my question now has to do with the facts, whether the facts contained in this paragraph change in any way your position, Mr. Butler, regarding the role of UNPROFOR in Potocari in connection with the evacuation and transportation of the population. I have to use these terms so as to avoid any legal terms such as "deportation."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure that I ever made a qualified opinion or judgement as to what I believed the Dutch were or were not doing in Potocari on the 12th and 13th with regards to the movement of the civilian population out of Potocari. I acknowledge that they're there; certainly the video footage shows that they're part of the process. The testimony and observations showing that they were disarmed as part of the process can infer that they clearly weren't seen as equals within the eyes of the VRS. But again, as I've not made an opinion as to what they are doing or not doing, I have no opinion to change in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You gave your opinion, Mr. Butler, on the basis of the meeting that took place, the presence of representatives of the Dutch Battalion, their Commander, General Karremans, and General Mladic, paragraph 4.4. And bearing in mind the fact that mention is made here of high officials of the United Nations, senior officials, does this have any bearing on the view that there was a previously prepared plan by the army of Republika Srpska for the transportation of the population or their evacuation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two issues there, and I'll respond to both of them. The first issue, in paragraph 4.4 of my report, I want to clarify that I'm not stating an opinion; I'm listing the facts. An opinion of what that is and what that means is not part of that. Now, responding to your second question, sir, as I've noted in my report and I'm not sure I've testified about it because I don't believe the Prosecution indicated it was germane for that, it has been my opinion and based on the fact basis and all of the other information to date, I certainly conclude that there were no prior plans for the movement of the Muslim population out of either Srebrenica or Potocari by buses as early as the evening of 11 July. Let me back off that just a bit. There were no visible, observable events that would indicate that. Where I qualify that is visible, observable pieces of information, the early morning message requesting buses from the Drina Corps units, the additional series of orders to the Minister of Defence that come out through the Main Staff pertaining to buses, those are observable instances which I use to qualify the judgement that there was no plan in existence. Now, moving back in time from that, it's very difficult to put a mark in the sand as to when at a point in time the army of Republika Srpska made a decision or was following a decision from the governmental leadership to execute that plan or begin to start putting the pieces together to execute that plan. The reflection of the facts that I have and the evidence that I have is that we start to see the manifestation of that in the early morning hours of 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the evidence at your disposal, was it, I think for the first time on the 9th of July, that the possibility is mentioned of the army of Republika Srpska entering Srebrenica, that is, the town itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, the evening of the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was it on the same date that the decision of the Muslim representatives of the civilian authorities that made the decision to abandon the town?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I disagree with that. If you are, in fact, referring to the prior exhibit that was shown, and I believe it's one of the footnotes to my report, it in no way, shape, or form, from my reading, indicates that a decision is made. What they're saying is that the members of the 28th Division of the ground forces are no longer able to prevent the aggressor forces from entering the town. They're asking for them, the BiH, to see if there's a possibility of opening a corridor to move the population. They need a reply in the next 24 hours, indicating that they hadn't made a decision yet if they're waiting for a reply. And as the information from Colonel Karremans that I believe was previously submitted to the Court indicates, he in fact met with those individuals during the evening hours of 10 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to Exhibit 404/2, footnote 41 [sic], for the record.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the correct exhibit, sir, just so I make sure I've got it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, it's all right. We don't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, speaking about the separation of men or, rather, the checks made by the Security Organs of the army of Republika Srpska to establish any possible criminal charges, can this be said to be a customary procedure under the circumstances that occurred in Srebrenica? I'm referring to the security checks made only?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the history of the area, where many aspects of military operations on both sides were frequently identified by the other side as being criminal in nature, the fact that we have a 12 July 1995 list from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade containing several hundred names, and the exact number escapes me at this moment, but it is dated 12 July 1995, certainly lends credence to the theory that in that particular instance, they were -- the security officers were conducting checks to -- or at least had the means to conduct the checks in so much as a listing of names of the Muslim males. Now, having noted that piece, that the means existed, the other side is that the events that occurred, as testified by the witnesses and some of the survivors, indicates that in most cases, individual identification of the Muslims were being destroyed by the soldiers in Potocari, which would have been counter-productive to the first purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if the liquidation of prisoners is part of the plan, is there any reasonable explanation why they would be moved from certain locations that are tens of kilometres away from Bratunac and brought to Bratunac, and then several days later from Bratunac, transported through the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, which is also tens of kilometres away, and then liquidated at locations which are quite well populated, doesn't it seem to you that this entire project, especially keeping prisoners at a location such as Bratunac, could have been called in question or compromised by the public, and as a result, the public would become aware of the intentions of those behind it? In other words, the intentions would be revealed to the public.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a real long series of questions, so again what I'll do is I'll deal with each specific issue in turn. If I understand the first part of the question, "moved from certain locations," and it says on my computer monitor "from Bratunac and then brought to Bratunac," and just to clarify, from Bratunac to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me make myself clearer. Is there any realistic or rational explanation why prisoners would be collected from various locations and brought to Bratunac, held there for several days, and then from Bratunac taken to the Zvornik Brigade zone, which again is dozens of kilometres away, and in relatively well-populated areas, executions carried out? So Bratunac could be described as a kind of collection centre from which then the prisoners were distributed to various other locations.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, yes, sir, that's exactly how I do identify Bratunac, as the initial collection centre. Going to, again, the first issue and setting aside the larger aspects of potential criminal intent and looking at this individual case strictly on an issue of logistics, as I've discussed, given a finite number of buses or resources to move the civilian population from Potocari, it's not unreasonable and my analysis is that the decision was made to move the civilian population out first. Now, clearly during the process, while you're moving the civilian population out over the longer stretch of road while those buses are moving, they're out of circulation longer, over the longer distance. If you play the numbers game, you can use a lot fewer buses shuttling prisoners over the relatively short distance, 10 kilometres, less than that, I believe, from Potocari to a collection site in Bratunac, then it would take -- if you wanted to move them simultaneously to the execution sites in Zvornik, but the first goal being get them out of Potocari. So in that respect, you can rather rapidly push them and put them into facilities in Bratunac with fewer resources than it would take to take them in buses and move them directly from Potocari to Zvornik at the same time. So in that case, technically speaking, the availability of logistics assets, again within determination of what the priority of movement for the people was, would play a significant factor, as would the availability of fuel. And certainly by the 13th and the 14th, the fact basis supports the fact that the VRS was very actively looking for fuel to continue. Moving to the next part of the question. They were in Bratunac as a collection centre, and as the fixed facilities filled up -- and we've talked about those fixed facilities, the hangar, the school -- prisoners who were taken along the Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road were placed and held in the transportation assets on the evening of the 13th. So in retrospect from a planning perspective, moving the civilian population out first was a smart move because if you had tried to do it at the same time, you would have run out of buses very quickly because you ran out of space to hold them in Bratunac. The third aspect that Mr. Petrusic indicated was that as you are putting all of these prisoners into Bratunac, certainly the civilian population is going to find out about what's going on just by sheer numbers alone, one would think. And further, as most of the survivors who were held in facilities in Bratunac indicate, there were, in fact, summary executions of a small scale, one or two or ten in some cases, occurring in that whole area. So certainly the sound of gunfire would have been alerting people. And I believe the investigation has indicated that many people in the Bratunac area were aware that Muslim prisoners were, in fact, being stored there. As I've noted in my narrative, I also discuss the issue that there is an intercept that we have between Miroslav Deronjic and an individual in the office of the President on, I believe, 14 July, although I'd have to verify the date, that indicates that Miroslav Deronjic understands that there's an awful lot of people in Bratunac, and he's receiving instructions from the office of the President that these people need to be moved out of there, get them out of warehouses. Now, we see the movement of those prisoners out of the Bratunac area starting the late afternoon -- or I'm sorry, starting the early evening of 13 July, and we see them moving into the zones of the Zvornik Brigade. And again, here I would defer with Defence counsel that the sites in question were not, in fact, public sites. They were, one, in generally remote areas; two, under military control; and far enough away from population areas that it would be relatively simple for the military to secure them away from the eyes of the general populace. In fact, logistically speaking, the most difficult part of the operation pertaining to public disclosure would have been the actual movement of the prisoners from Bratunac to those locations, because during that, that's where they would have had to transit the municipality -- or the actual city of Zvornik, that's where they would have come through, the civilian population. So in that regards, the actual sites where they were holding these prisoners wouldn't qualify as public as all; it would qualify as a relatively isolated facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The cultural centre in Pilica, is it not in the very centre of that town? Can it be said that the Pilica Cultural Centre is in the centre of the town of Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that it is in the centre of town, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I know that it's not easy to speak about this whole situation. I don't -- I hate to use the word, but it -- the "plan," but if it was all a part of the plan, if indeed one can talk about a plan, would it not have been easier to liquidate the prisoners in the collection areas, at the very spot where they were rounded up, which was far away from the public eye? Let me take the example of Sandici.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, my understanding is that, at least on one individual case, that there was one, maybe more, executions at Sandici. Further extrapolating that, several hundred of the prisoners from Sandici were, in fact, marched to and executed in the Kravica warehouse, again, in a public place. Kravica warehouse and, to some extent, the Pilica Dom, as you've noted, are public places and stand out as significant differences to the more private executions that occurred in other locations. Now, the difficult part, as you noted, for me is trying to take those two different circumstances which resulted in mass executions and fold out how those fell back into the plan, and I don't know that I can make that leap from point "A" to point "B," sir. I could speculate a lot, but it would mean very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your general view and the conclusion about the issue, is it true to say that the units which participated in the capture had as their assignment to collect, to round up, or physically capture the Muslims, and to hand them over for transport in the direction of Bratunac? Was that their only assignment, and is it true that they, bearing that in mind, wouldn't know anything about their fate after that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, several questions, and let me take them in turn. Was that their only assignment? The units, and for the sake of this discussion I believe we're talking about the units along the road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba, they had two missions at the time: The function of engaging the column as it was going past, and as part of that function, dealing with Muslims who had surrendered or who had been captured from that column. As the Dutch witnesses and other witnesses who were part of that process have previously testified, in many cases, there were summary executions of one or two or several along the road as those were occurring. And certainly, as the Dutch soldiers went by and certainly some of the other survivors went by, there were bodies on the road. Certainly Kravica warehouse happens at approximately 1700 on 13 July. We have a mass execution that occurs in the Cerska Valley sometime during the afternoon of the 13 July, and we have several smaller killings, the Jadar River killing and things of that nature, that are all occurring on 13 July along that road. So again, trying not to put myself into the mental state of individual soldiers or small unit commanders who were putting people on buses and sending them to Bratunac, I'm not sure that I would make the conclusion that these individuals had no idea or would not have any idea what would be happening to those Muslims at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to suggest a break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will accept your proposal gladly, Mr. Petrusic. We will have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before we continue with the examination of the witness, Mr. Visnjic pointed out to me an error. Page 37, line 21 on the transcript, Exhibit 404/2, instead "footnote number 41," there should be "footnote 73."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you have any knowledge as to whether there was any other unit from the 65th Regiment, apart from the military police, which was located in Nova Kasaba, that is, whether there was any other unit located in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one direction of the road, I believe on a map it's further to the west, you have Milici, the headquarters of the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade, and moving the other direction up the road you have the headquarters of the 5th Engineer Regiment -- I'm sorry, I believe it's 5th Engineer Battalion of the Drina Corps at Konjevic Polje. Further, at Konjevic Polje, there are some indications that one or two elements of MUP Special Police or MUP municipal police were at the Konjevic Polje location as early as March as a result of the thinning of the lines in that area, and the MUP was requested by the army to take over some of the military security-related functions on the terrain. I believe this MUP unit moved in, the documents indicate, in March of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the 65th Protection Regiment, does it have a motorised battalion amongst its members? Do you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the 65th Protection Regiment is that there is at least one motorised battalion. However, that would not be at Nova Kasaba. My understanding is that those units were garrisoned on the other side of Han Pijesak and, in effect, were protecting the Main Staff headquarters which was located, in that distance, very close to the Muslim enclave at Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, was there any reason for this mechanised battalion be put into usage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific about the time frame, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period of time between -- rather as of the 11th of July and then onwards until the end of July. So was there any reason for that battalion to be deployed during that period of time outside the Han Pijesak location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that the unit was deployed and became part of the operation to take Zepa, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Butler, which evidence leads to the conclusion that as regards the wider area of Potocari, the presence of the units of Sreten Petrovic was observed, Sreten Petrovic being the Deputy Commander of the 3rd Battalion, and also the presence of Zoran Kovacevic, the Commander of the 4th Company of the 2nd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Zoran Kovacevic, we have the video still with his name captioned as Zoran Kovacevic and the identification from the roster of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade that he is the Company Commander of -- the fourth Company Commander of the 2nd Battalion. In the case of Sreten Petrovic, we identify him by position first in the 10 July 1995 Bratunac daily combat report, and when I say "identify" I mean in a chronological sense with regards to this, where he's indicated that he had been wounded. And further, one of the witnesses, and off the top of my head I won't speculate which witness it is, indicates -- or I think two of them indicate, in the case of Petrovic -- they give identifications, which putting the two together, lead me to conclude that that was Sreten Petrovic in Potocari. Further, the identification of Sreten Petrovic is noted in the interview that was conducted with Serbian reporter Zoran Petrovic, where he specifically notes Sreten Petrovic also being in Bratunac during that period, although I do not believe he specifically designates which day Sreten Petrovic is in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Butler, we can note the presence of the two of them personally, and we have evidence to prove that. Is there any evidence that would indicate that the units under their command were present in the same area and during the same time frame?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the 13 July 1995 videotape of the events that are occurring in Potocari show a large number of soldiers in the area, and some of them, the soldiers, clearly in green uniforms and armed, are in positions relative to the buses. But the specific task of placing those soldiers within the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, I do not have the specificity of evidence that can make that conclusion. I only conclude their presence by the presence of the Commander, the presence of an individual from the 2nd Battalion who is in a leadership position, a Company Commander, and the fact that given the other events that we know occurred on the battlefield at the time, or at least relative to positional unit locations, it would be logical that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to an assertion that was made in respect of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. Although I know it's quite difficult to judge, but is it true that when it comes to the mentality of the commanding officers, bearing in mind the fact that they are from the area, that they as individuals wanted to be present there for certain reasons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, getting into the mental state of a specific commander on the ground, I assume we're talking about these two individuals. In the case of these two individuals, certainly there would be a reason why they would want to be there, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
