utterances.text: Is there any evidence which would indicate that one can reach a reliable conclusion as to who was in charge of securing the positions -- or rather, the locations where the prisoners were being held on in Bratunac as of the 13th of July? I am referring both to fixed facilities and the means of transport which were taking them there.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the variety of the circumstances that are occurring, and the fact that the resources that are part of the process come from over and above the Bratunac Brigade's own limited resources, and the coordination part with the municipality of Bratunac for facilities, and all of the other things that had to have occurred in order to store these people to include the period of the 13th of July, my conclusion is that it would have had to have been at a level of the Drina Corps Command, specifically, the person who would have been responsible for dealing with a lot of the prisoner specific issues, the Assistant Commander for Security, Colonel Popovic; but as I've noted in previous testimony, other aspects involved as well, including the logistical issue regarding the Drina Corps rear staff, Colonel Acimovic and his soldiers, and within the context of this, the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6.11 you note under the heading "Specific Observations: Of note, in many instances, it is clear from the overall pattern that many Serb soldiers knew the identities of Muslim prisoners whom they had lived with before the war." Assuming that the town of Bratunac is an urban area in which the civilian authorities have a number of certain competencies, and that includes the military -- the civilian police as well, would it be logical to say that the civilian police in such an urban area would conduct or provide for the security of the prisoners who were being killed in these facilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that at all, sir. The military regulations and the customary practice places that responsibility primarily on military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Bratunac Brigade structurally speaking did not have a military police, but that the Brigade Commander had the right to establish such a formation, which he did indeed establish, with these forces, military police forces, would it be possible to secure such a large number of prisoners in these locations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of the Bratunac Brigade Military Police, because of the notations in their daily orders journal, one of the observations that I make in both my report and, I believe, in testimony is the fact that the roles that they're performing revolve around providing security for General Mladic, security for the UN forces, and security of the -- or security of the Bratunac medical centre, which of course at that time is filling up with wounded Muslim civilians and military personnel as well, wounded military personnel who are Muslims. I don't want to make an artificial distinction there. So we know what the Bratunac military police are doing during that period, sir. Getting back to the larger scope, given the scale, the sheer scale of the amount of prisoners who were being collected in Bratunac, even if they were not performing that function, I would think that it would be unlikely that that platoon would be able to secure the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Under the assumption that they were being secured by them in addition to the military police platoon, they were also secured by someone else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would you have any knowledge and information as to what other elements may have been involved in that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Getting back to the specific observation that I made in paragraph 6.11, noting that many of the survivors knew or had observed the pattern that Serb soldiers knew them because they had lived with them before the war, what I do then is I take that and I use the word "implies," that the units responsible for guarding the Muslims in the town were from the local base unit, the Bratunac Brigade. I make that implication, and I acknowledge that that's what I'm making it on. I don't have additional information which would be able to make that a more firmer conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that, could the units guarding them have been the units of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my understanding, again, from information developed by the investigation team, that Bratunac civilian police were not involved in the guarding of the prisoners and were, in many cases, up along the road from Bratunac towards Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The 5th Engineer Battalion that you referred to earlier on, was that a combat unit of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the US army, for the most part, tactical engineers are considered to be a combat formation. I don't know that within the VRS, that they make that distinction along the same lines that we do, so because of that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It was also located at Nova Kasaba, a little further away from the 65th Protection Regiment -- or rather, the military police. Was it natural to expect that unit to have its own security on a permanent basis, and especially during the time when the column is moving from Srebrenica in the direction of the zone of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I'm sorry, Nova Kasaba is not the location of the 5th Engineer Battalion. It is, in fact, located at Konjevic Polje. Relative to your comment or question on security, the engineers as soldiers would in effect, like all other soldiers, be providing for their own security in many cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your specific observations and at paragraph 6.20, you refer to the 1st Infantry Battalion commanded by Lieutenant Lazar Ostoric and the 4th Infantry Battalion commanded by Captain 1st Class Radika Petrovic. Could you, although I know it's very difficult, tell us which region, which zone they secured, these two battalions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two battalions, and as I indicated, and perhaps maybe the best way to do this is to pull out the map exhibit, and then rather than me try to verbally explain it, it would just be easier to point to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I would be quite agreeable to that, but I'm not sure which exhibit number that map has. I think on this map, one could point to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 498 [sic], Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. We have seen an example of good cooperation between the two parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I too should like to thank Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Apparently that's 485. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As identified on the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Butler. [In English] Could you move it to the side so Mr. Petrusic can follow. I don't know if it's possible or not. In a way that the Prosecution can see too.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for making this so hard. Maybe I shouldn't have asked for the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As indicated on this map, the 1st Battalion boundary location's just to the west of Bratunac to this area south of Glogova, and the 4th Battalion, during the period along the enclave actually ran along the former enclave boundary. Now, what happened relative to the events of 12 and 13 July 1995, was that as the column was moving out, the units in fact came up to the road. In effect, the road became the forward line of troops from this position here out. And for other units, 1st, 2nd Battalion, starting on the 14th, after the events of the 13th had occurred, the units went back in and started conducting sweep operations. So this, based on the information we have, is a relatively accurate portrayal of those battalion positions. The one item that is undesignated is where the western or right-hand boundary in case -- or left-hand boundary in this case, looking at it your way, of the 4th Battalion boundary ends and where another formation picks it up. We don't get a firm designation of the 4th Battalion boundary until the 14 July OP order by the Bratunac Brigade which established them operating through Sandici. Do you need me at the map more, sir, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I was interested in learning whether we have any knowledge about the neighbouring unit to the 4th Battalion to the left-hand side, but obviously we do not have that information.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, what we don't have is where the boundary is. We do understand and the investigation has indicated and the other information, the evidence, indicates that MUP forces were operating to the west along the road from an undesignated area towards Konjevic Polje. So while I can't place a military unit there, the evidence to include Bratunac daily combat reports indicate that MUP units were out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, please correct me if I'm wrong, but if I understand you correctly, you said that on the road, Kravica to Konjevic Polje, there were MUP units present. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elements of the Ministry of the Interior police units are noted along the road in both the daily combat reports and are also observed along the road as part of the 13 July 1995 Petrovic video.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are the units on the Petrovic video the ones wearing flak jackets as part of their equipment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to the exhibits tendered, the specific photograph that I tendered relative to flak jackets, those individuals I identify as army members. Looking at other photographs of the MUP soldiers that are out there from the stills that we have from the video, many of them do not appear to have flak jackets. Some of them may be wearing flak jackets underneath other clothing that's not plainly visible. So with that regard, I wouldn't make the qualification that MUP units were or were not 1 2 3 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts wearing flak jackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In an infantry brigade or at a lower level, an infantry battalion, do battalion members have, as a component part of their equipment, such flak jackets?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that if they didn't have them, they would want them. But looking to the situation specific to Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade, as we have their documents, we note that the Zvornik Brigade has, as part of their inventories, a large number of flak jackets, as is reflected. We know that in the case of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, not only did they apparently not have flak jackets, they did not have helmets. So while I'm not sure whether or not, formationally speaking, infantry battalions within the former JNA and VRS are specifically entitled to have forms of ballistic protection jackets, flak jackets, as part of their organisational equipment, certainly if the units could get a hold of them, the soldiers were wearing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In normal conditions in the army of Republika Srpska, this was not a component part of the equipment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have enough information pertaining to the entire scope of the Army of Republika Srpska to answer that question positively or negatively, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that the Zvornik Brigade had in its possession some of that equipment. According to what we could see on the video, the Petrovic video as well as others, was a part of that equipment being used by members of the so-called elite units of the Zvornik Brigade under the command of Jolovic, that is, the Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly as the video demonstrates and as previous video exhibits note also, the members of the Drina Wolves, the Podrinje Detachment, had in many cases or were seen in many cases wearing those forms of ballistic protection. But as the Petrovic video indicates, other soldiers had them as well. It was not exclusive to any elite unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Butler, we exclude Drina Wolves from this location, Konjevic Polje-Kasaba. They were not seen in that area, were they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have one indication from a witness who, on 13 July 1995, observes a van which that witness indicates has the insignia of a Drina Wolf on it. That is the only report or the only piece of information that I have of a Drina Wolf unit or somebody identifying somebody of the Drina Wolves in that area. I would just specify, since I don't see it on the transcript, that that location was identified at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No, not Nova Kasaba but on the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba was my question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe the witness was that specific. He says at Nova Kasaba. I don't believe he specifies whether it's on the road prior or not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: There obviously seems to be a misunderstanding between us, Mr. Butler. Mr. Butler, on what grounds do you make the conclusion that the Intelligence and Security Organ of the Bratunac Brigade designated Kravica as the place where the prisoners would be held and informed lower-level units about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, I believe you're referring to paragraph 6.25 of my report, and again I note that related to the fact base that inferences can be drawn, several of them in this case. The inferences that I draw based on the totality of the situation as I understand it and the fact basis, and I believe I've gone over that in my direct testimony so I won't revisit that whole area, indicate that with the units of the Bratunac Brigade operating there primarily, that they would have privacy for particularly some of the prisoner operations there. Again, the inference that prisoners were being assembled at Kravica and as a result somebody had to have designated Kravica, the warehouse, as a collection location, and somebody had to have transmitted that out to the other formations, and at the end of the paragraph 6.25, I note that it should have been a function of the Intelligence and Security Branch of the Bratunac Brigade. I can't specifically conclude that it was, and I believe that I note that I can't conclude specifically that it was in my report; but I note that it should have been their job and function to do that based on all of the other facts surrounding those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we've come to chapter 7 or 7.0 of your report. Can it be said that the depth of the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, that that territory was far removed from the combat positions and operations in relation to the locations where executions were taking place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that as part of the report and, again, as part of my direct testimony I've identified the locations where the executions took place and showed, particularly with respect to the execution sites at Orahovac, Petkovci, Branjevo Military Farm, and Kozluk, where those locations are -- I'm sorry, and Pilica Dom, where those locations are relative to the combat that I understand was occurring on those given days, sir. So I don't want to make a general blanket statement that it's near or far; I believe I've been very specific about it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So that is your final reply to my question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reply is that as part of the report and my testimony, I've been very specific as to the locations. Your question was, would I agree that it's near or far, and again, with respect to the location of the execution site and the combat on any given day, the answer is situation dependent. I've qualified those in my report and my direct testimony exactly where the combat was occurring at a given time, and placed the physical location of the execution site where it is in respect of that combat. So again, rather than talk in a broad generality, I believe I've specifically designated where the sites are in relation to the combats on a given day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler, I'm certainly not disputing that, so allow me to go on to my next question. In your opinion, Mr. Butler, the Command of the Zvornik Brigade in his report dated 18 July to the Drina Corps Command, does he know about the fate of the prisoners who were held in schools in his zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one reads the 18 July interim combat report, and when you read it in conjunction with his previously-authored 15 July interim combat report discussing the issue of security obligations and terrain restoration, I can conclude that he was aware of the fate of the people in those schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The restoration of the terrain, that is a parameter, is it a determinant on the basis of which you come to that conclusion? Is it an element in the process of conclusion that you make?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elements pertaining to the conclusion that I make are not based on one specific statement or one specific phrase. The elements that I base my conclusion pertain to the broad reading of the 15 July interim report; the fact that when you look at it in time sequence, that Colonel Pandurevic is just arriving into the zone of his brigade and has been in the zone of his brigade for less than six hours when that report is written; the fact that he very rapidly becomes aware of what's going on, to a point where he's in a position to articulate what's going on, on the 15th in the interim report; given the fact that he further articulates numbers on the 18th of July; putting those all together, along with all of the other fact-based information that's out there, that is what I draw my conclusion on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, written traces and reports on crimes committed, with the exception of the regular and interim reports of the Zvornik Brigade to the Drina Corps Command, do not exist, do they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you define the commission of the crime as the actual period between 15 and 18, I would again remind you that we have two reports that exist during that period. If you expand the elements of the crime out beyond that, we have several pieces of information which further amplify that going into September when they're actually involved in the process of the reburial of the bodies. So again, laying out information, it does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, perhaps I cannot phrase this as a question, but I keep trying to find out why Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic would be sending a report saying that he didn't know what to do with the 3.000 Muslims housed in schools when they had obviously by then already been liquidated.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, sir, you're reading both reports out of time context. The 15 July interim combat report identifies the fact that his unit is involved with obligations of security and terrain restoration. At that time that that report is sent on 15 July, the prisoners had already been executed at Orahovac and Petkovci. They were still alive. According to survivor accounts and the information derived from the investigation, in the areas of Pilica, Pilica Dom, and possibly the school at Rocevic. Those executions, for the most part, did not occur until the 16th, with, again, the possible exception of Kozluk which may have occurred as early as 15 July. We don't know, and certainly I can't tell from documents on that. On the 18th of July after the completion of all of the executions, of all the mass executions in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, it is at that point that Colonel Pandurevic identifies the number 3.000 and associates it with Muslims who were held in schools in the Zvornik municipality, his zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic, I think that this would be an appropriate moment for a break. I think a quarter of an hour will be sufficient, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we are now on the Exhibit number 609.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In this regular combat report, Commander Pandurevic says that: "This command can no longer take care of these problems because it does not have -- as it has neither the material nor other resources. If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." In your opinion, Mr. Butler, if there is a plan to liquidate -- a plan for liquidation which the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade is familiar, would he submit such a report to his Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the circumstances that were occurring in the zone at the time and bringing it back several days, and as I've previously noted in both my report and direct testimony, when you look at the movement of the column and the size of the column, it appears that looking at the totality of the information, the only people who really had an accurate feel for how dangerous the column was to the zone would be the Deputy Commander of the Zvornik Brigade at the time, Major Obrenovic. And as reflected in the intercepts and written reports culminating with the interim report on 14 July, he is very urgently requesting the return and assistance of corps units because of the developing danger. And again as I note both in my report and in direct testimony, the general impression is that the remainder of the Drina Corps is playing down the threat. They don't believe Dragan Obrenovic, that it is as serious as it is. Certainly they become aware by 14 July, in the evening hours. It is an extremely significant threat. And again, we've gone over that as part of my cross-examination, just how significant the threat was, how it was perceived to be to him. Putting it back in the context of a plan, again understanding that the plan involved the movement of people up from Bratunac, understanding that the plan involved putting them in several locations, going back in time to when a decision must have been made to do that, prior to the actual understanding of how dangerous this column was and what type of military threat it represented. So here you have the plan of executing these people on mass scale on one hand, you have the developing threat of the column getting closer to the Zvornik Brigade, and they didn't anticipate the column, and they certainly didn't anticipate how significant a threat it was to them. Certainly within the scale of the corps, the Zvornik Brigade, on the other hand, saying, "This is significant. We need help." So understanding that is the scope of the context and then looking at this on 15 July 1995, Colonel Pandurevic understanding both of those factors, it's completely reasonable that he'd send a report like that to the Corps Commander, essentially telling the Corps Commander, "I can fight the column. I can execute the prisoners. I can't do both simultaneously, somebody has got to handle something." And within that context, that's how I come to the opinion and that's how I make that particular conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Major Obrenovic and, later on, Colonel Pandurevic, on the 14th or, rather, on the 15th of July, are taking care of the breakthrough of the Muslim column. This specifically concerns Major Obrenovic on the 13th and the 14th of July. On the 14th of July, in the morning hours, the column of Muslim prisoners is moving from Bratunac towards the locations in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. We do not have any information, any evidence, or rather let me put it this way: Is there any evidence which would indicate that Major Obrenovic is indeed informed at least about that fact, the fact that the column of Muslim prisoners will be placed in the locations where they were eventually placed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, what you've asked is do I have a specific piece of information that indicates that Major Obrenovic knew that the prisoners were being placed in those specific locations. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a specific piece of information that says that. What I have is the picture that I build relative to the larger context, the fact that the Military Police Company or elements of that company go to Orahovac, the fact that the Engineer Company is at Orahovac during and after the execution. Certainly Major Obrenovic was responsible for placing the military police in the lines and the ambush positions on 12 and 13 July, and certainly in one specific instance I have information that Major Obrenovic was aware that the Commander of the military police was removed from those lines on the late evening of the 13th of July, 1995. And as the log of the Military Police Company indicates, him and 13 other people were at Orahovac on the 14th, starting late evening of the 13th through the 14th. So while I do not have a specific piece of paper that indicates that Major Obrenovic knew, I have a lot of inferences, and one specific fact that he knew that his police commander was pulled off the lines. In fact, he pulled him off the lines and reports him going to the standard facility. So that, coupled with the fact that, again, Colonel Pandurevic arriving in the zone after being at Zepa from the early morning hours of -- or late evening hours of 13 July, early morning hours of 14 July, and being out of the zone of the Zvornik Brigade since essentially 6 July, comes back into the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, rather quickly gets an appreciation for what is specifically going on in his entire zone, to include an awareness of security obligations and terrain restoration, somebody had to have informed Colonel Pandurevic of all those things. Major Obrenovic as the Deputy Commander of the brigade, Colonel Pandurevic's Chief of Staff, and arguably the most knowledgeable person of what's going on in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade during that period, is the logical person who would have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Pandurevic returns to his area only because of the combat activities with the column of Muslims who was moving through. That was the only reason for his return to his area.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was that the most dominant and the only reason of his return?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would certainly be the most pressing reason why he would return, but I could not possibly speculate as to other reasons why he may have returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you had access to a large number of documents of the Bratunac and the Zvornik Brigades; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are among the many sources of information I had access to, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade is also the town of Bratunac itself, as you have stated.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Taking into account all available materials that you had access to, is there any document on the basis of which the Commander of the Bratunac Brigade, his Chief of Staff, informs the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade or his Chief of Staff that in his area of responsibility, a couple of thousands of prisoners will be coming, that he's expecting the arrival of several thousands of prisoners in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade Commander physically located in his zone, the Chief of Staff of the Bratunac Brigade accompanying the unit down to Bracan, Colonel Pandurevic who until the morning, or certainly the afternoon, early evening hours of 13 of July, is still in the zone of the Bratunac Brigade, and Major Obrenovic in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, and I only just note that because I want to place their physical locations on the ground. Having done that, no, I don't have any written piece of information that notes that, but realistically speaking, and given how I understand the Drina Corps to work and how a corps operating methodology works, that would not be the responsibility of the brigade to do that. That would, in fact, be the responsibility of the corps staff to coordinate those actions between two subordinate brigades. And if you review paragraph 7.3 of chapter 7, one of the few pieces of information that we have that we can infer to be part of that planning process is the travels of a military police vehicle from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade to various sites which later become holding sites, and one of those trips on 13 July is down to Bratunac. So specifically in answer to your question, between those four correspondence, the answer is "no," but I wouldn't expect the answer to be "yes" given the situation and the roles and responsibilities of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you want to say, then, that this particular activity, the transfer from the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade to the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility, is taking place at the level of the corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expand that more than just the actual transfer from point "A" to point "B." The entire programme represents coordinated activity between the brigade Commands and the corps Command, as the higher headquarters, and clearly in response to directives from the Superior Command, that being General Mladic. This is -- the entire scope of this type of an operation doesn't happen in isolation; it all is happening in response to something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the documentation of the Drina Corps, at least in accordance with what you say, is something that you were not in the position to study. Would that be a correct statement? At least, a large portion of that documentation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've noted previously, certainly in direct testimony, we do not have the Drina Corps records and documents that we knew or know should have reflected their activities during this time period. We have over the series of last couple of years been requesting that material, and as the Court understands, a series of those documents are subject to Court-directed binding orders for production. The last word that we have received, again, comes from the RS Minister of Defence, indicating that those documents are not available. So within that context, I know that there is, in fact, material out there; I know that I don't have access to it. And what I've tried to do, based on the material that I do have, is try to construct a map or a series of documents that I know that the Drina Corps did send that other agencies did receive based on order numbers. So I think I have a good idea of what I'm missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you had access to in terms of documentation of the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigade, and perhaps the orders of the Drina Corps issued to the brigades at a lower level of command, and both regular and interim reports, is it possible to say -- is it possible for you to say with certainty that the Drina Corps and its command staff participated in these -- in all this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have made that a conclusion of my report, yes, sir. I do not believe that this could have occurred as an organised programme that we see it to be without the Drina Corps and its staff's participation. And certainly as we've gone through in direct and, in some cases, cross-examination, the physical identities of many of the Drina Corps staff members who were part of that programme tends to confirm that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we've now come to paragraph 8.43 of your report, where you say: "In reviewing the period prior to the 13th of July 1995, it is clear that General Major Krstic was not only functioning as the Drina Corps Chief of Staff, but he was probably also functioning as the operational Commander for the military forces grouped together for operation Krivaja-95." Is there any evidence that an operational group was formed for the operation Krivaja-95 and that the operational Commander was General Major Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what we have in this case is again a translational terminology issue between the English language military term and the military term as translated into B/C/S. My identification of him is the Operational Commander, is as he is the Commander of the grouped military forces that is conducting the operation. And with that regard, and we've had this previous discussion before on what that means as, you know, the Commander of that grouping, that's the function that he performed. That is not to be confused with, in the B/C/S language, in the military terminology, a formal operational grouping it's called, which in the JNA, as adopted by the VRS military terminology and practice, is a grouping of several units from other formations, and it represents a formalised grouping with a formalised designated Commander and a formal designated staff and that lasts for a designated time. So in this case, I'm referring to the role of General Krstic performing as the Commander of this grouping of forces, not as General Krstic, the Commander of a formalised operational grouping within the terminology of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My understanding was, as you have just said, and my question was put accordingly, but even if he is the Commander of the group carrying out combat operations within the framework of the operation Krivaja-95, in that case is an order necessary whereby Major General Krstic will be authorised to carry out that operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering within the context that he's the second senior ranking individual in the Drina Corps, that the brigades would be functionally under his control for many aspects of that anyway, I wouldn't see a required necessity to do that. And if one looks at the operations order for the Zepa operation, those same types of things are done, yet General Krstic is not specifically designated as the Commander, if memory serves me. Now, having said that, it would have been prudent for that to have occurred, but it's not a necessity, no, sir. Certainly not for operations conducted within the zone of the corps that he has a formalised position of responsibility in already. Now, if that type of situation were to exist where you had multiple corps units and things of that nature involved, then certainly I would expect to see that to reflect a very clear chain of command for units that are coming outside from other locations so there is no confusion. And when I use the phrase "multiple corps" -- I see it just came up on the transcript -- I'm not talking multiple corps units within the framework of one corps. What I would be giving as an example would be a unit coming in from Sarajevo, Romanjia Brigade or the Hercegovina Corps, something -- multiple corps, in a plural sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that he was Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander, for an execution of an operation of this kind and if the command function were to be entrusted to him for that operation, would it be necessary, according to the regulations and the system of military control and command, for him to be so authorised either by the Corps Commander or the Commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the implied command authority is derived from the Corps Commander, the presumption being if the Corps Commander did not want General Krstic to be doing this, the Corps Commander would not have put him in the position to do it. So with that regard, certainly he's operating under the control of the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, did your studies establish that a statement by president -- that the statement by President Karadzic is correct and that it supports this thesis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If memory serves me correctly, the comments made by President Karadzic -- and if possible I'd like to see them just so I don't make an error in memory. I think I'll wait for that, because you can probably understand there are about 5.000 documents going both ways in my mind, and I don't want to make an error in memory on this one. I believe it was tendered as the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we should be able to come up with that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Mr. Petrusic, you can go on to another question, and as soon as we find the exhibit, you can come back to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, I think we have that, Mr. President. It's Exhibit 99, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now you can put your question, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: President Karadzic stated, and let me paraphrase, that Krstic planned the operation in front of him and he approved it. Apart from the video, do you have possession of that evidence or, rather, has your investigation established that President Karadzic's statement was correct, that is, that it reflects the facts and the evidence in your possession? Does that evidence corroborate this statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I have is broadly corroborated. I mean, the statement is broadly corroborated by that. As to the specifics, can I corroborate the fact that President Karadzic was accurate in his recollection when he made that statement, I cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, regardless of Karadzic's statement, can you, on the basis of your analytical studies, say that you reached the conclusion that General Krstic planned the operation Krivaja-95?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering his personal involvement in the aspects of the military operation as they occurred, considering that as the Corps Chief of Staff it would have been his primary responsibility to oversee all aspects of the planning of the operation, I conclude that he, in fact, was responsible for much of the planning if not all of the planning for the military context. Now, that's not to say that he planned every specific detail. He may not have even written the plan himself, composed of his own hand, but the plan is a reflection of the work of the staff officers of the Drina Corps of which he is the functional coordinator and controller of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you use the word "plan," I assume you mean for the Krivaja operation or the combat order for active combat deployment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring in this respect to the Krivaja-95 plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have another two or three minutes until the end of our planned time, and the Defence would like to go on to the last part of its cross-examination of Mr. Butler, and we assume that we will be able to finish the cross by the first break tomorrow, and that is why I would now suggest that we adjourn for lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, Mr. Petrusic. I think it is a good suggestion. We're going to stop for today, and we will resume work tomorrow at 9.30 to continue your cross-examination. You said it is your last section. Does that mean in private session? So we'll be here tomorrow at 9.30, but for the information of the public, we'll be working in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. The Defence will continue to cross-examine in open session, and at the very end we will request a private session; but most part of the cross-examination will take place in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, then. So we'll be continuing under normal conditions, that is, in open session tomorrow at 9.30. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: be reconvened on Friday the 21st day of July, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
